ai_boosting: A useful way to describe it is that each added tree responds to what the current ensemble still gets wrong under its training objective. That is a property of the algorithm, not an explanation of why a specific Bandung day was misclassified. Our paper evaluates the resulting classifier, not the contribution of every individual tree.
ai_additive: The trees are not separate forecasts that we vote on equally. Their outputs accumulate, with the learning rate limiting each new contribution. The paper's 300-tree setting therefore describes model capacity, but it does not tell us which particular tree or split explains a rain prediction. For that we used aggregate model metrics and separate explanation methods.
ai_gradient_hessian: If you want a concrete picture, the gradient points to a direction in which the current prediction should change, and the Hessian helps quantify how strongly the objective bends locally. They are calculated from the training loss, not measured by BMKG. Because the exact internal objective was not specified in the paper, I would explain this as general XGBoost mechanics.
ai_training_objective: I would separate two levels: the internal objective used to build trees and the external score used to choose among trained configurations. We can verify the latter was F1 from the reported grid search. We should not invent the exact internal objective or imply the algorithm optimized thresholded F1 directly unless the original code confirms it.
ai_f1_nondifferentiable: The distinction matters because the final F1 depends on class labels after a cutoff, while tree fitting updates continuous model scores. Grid search can train several candidate models and then calculate F1 from their validation predictions. This is standard model selection logic, but our paper does not document every internal optimization setting.
ai_gain_split: A high gain feature was useful to this fitted tree system for reducing its objective at the places where it split. It might be a proxy for another correlated variable, so the ranking can shift when the feature pool changes. That is why comparing gain with LIME is informative, but neither ranking alone proves a physical causal mechanism.
ai_importance_types: For example, a variable might appear in many small improvements and score highly by split count, while another appears in a few very valuable splits and scores highly by gain. The paper used one defined gain summary for Path B. We did not claim that the same feature order would hold under cover or every other importance definition.
ai_depth: A depth limit changes the kinds of conditional rules an individual tree can represent. Shallower trees generally restrict complex combinations of weather inputs, which can help keep a small dataset from fitting noise. However, depth three was selected within the reported search; we did not perform a separate experiment proving that three was the uniquely best depth.
ai_learning_rate: A small step size can make boosting less abrupt, but it must be considered together with the number of trees. Too few trees at that rate could underfit, and too many could still overfit. The selected pair was applied consistently across the three paths; the paper does not show a full learning curve or sensitivity analysis for that pair.
ai_subsample: This sampling happens during training, not when the model receives a new weather day for prediction. The point is to expose each tree to a subset of rows and potentially reduce reliance on quirks of the training sample. Because we did not ablate subsample independently, I would avoid claiming a measured improvement specifically caused by 0.8.
ai_colsample: Column sampling changes which predictors each tree can consider, which matters when humidity-related features share information. It is a training regularization choice, not a statement that 20% of weather variables are permanently removed from the model. All three paths used the same setting, so the reported comparison does not isolate its individual contribution.
ai_overfit: A later hold-out and forward-time folds are stronger checks than training accuracy alone. Still, similar validation scores do not establish that the model is free of overfitting, especially when feature selection and tuning are not fully nested. A stronger check would report training-versus-validation curves and repeat the entire selection process inside each fold.
ai_early_stopping: I would answer this as a reporting limit rather than guess. We know the selected configuration included 300 trees, but the paper does not say that a validation metric stopped training early. If early stopping were added, its validation window must come from the training period; using the final hold-out to choose a stopping point would contaminate the evaluation.
ai_xgb_missing: Native missing-value routing and explicit imputation are different modeling choices. Imputation also affects derived weather features and the explanation inputs, so the choice should be kept consistent across the paths. We did not run a head-to-head experiment between these approaches. The safe claim is what the pipeline actually did, plus the need for a sensitivity test.
ai_tree_probability: For a user, the important difference is between a model score and a trustworthy forecast probability. A value of 0.491 fell below the 0.5 class threshold in the documented December case, but that does not tell us whether the model is calibrated over many days. Reliability diagrams or calibration scores would be needed before treating 49.1% as a literal observed rain frequency.
ai_lime_acronym: The word local is essential: one explanation describes the neighborhood of one input, not the entire global behavior of the classifier. Model-agnostic means it can query predictions without reading XGBoost's tree structure. In our experiment we aggregated many such local explanations for refinement, and that extra aggregation requires its own interpretation and caution.
ai_lime_steps: The final weights are properties of the fitted local surrogate and its sampled neighborhood. If the perturbation distribution, distance weighting, or random seed changes, the explanation may also change. We therefore checked seed stability of the aggregate ranking, but we did not report a separate local-fidelity score for each day.
ai_lime_surrogate: It helps to call the surrogate a local approximation rather than a transparent copy of XGBoost. Its coefficient can be useful for discussing one prediction, but only if the approximation fits nearby model outputs well. This paper reports ranking stability, not a dedicated fidelity benchmark, so I would not say the surrogate was proven exact.
ai_lime_kernel: The chosen neighborhood defines what local means in practice. If it is too broad, the surrogate can blend different parts of a nonlinear decision surface; if it is too narrow, it may depend heavily on a small set of synthetic points. The paper fixed the LIME setup and did not establish an optimal kernel width.
ai_lime_modelagnostic: This flexibility is the reason LIME could be compared with a built-in XGBoost explanation. It also means the method sees model outputs through a designed sample of nearby inputs, not the underlying meteorological mechanism. So we should discuss its local faithfulness and the realism of perturbations separately from its portability.
ai_lime_perturbation: For example, independently varying humidity and a humidity-derived dew-point feature can produce combinations that would rarely occur in actual weather. XGBoost will still return a number for such an input, and LIME may fit that behavior. Our study did not measure how frequent these unrealistic neighbors were, so the weights remain model diagnostics, not physical interventions.
ai_lime_bins: The bins are calculated from the reference data. Their boundaries can therefore move if the dataset changes, and a number near a boundary may receive a different explanation label even when the physical weather changes only slightly. That is why we describe the reported humidity cutoffs as explanation categories rather than universal meteorological thresholds.
ai_lime_weight_sign: The class being explained matters: a weight for rain should not be casually interpreted as the same sign for no rain. The weight is also local to an input and to the surrogate's approximation. For a physical claim about changing humidity, we would need a different design that addresses correlated variables and causal assumptions.
ai_lime_abs: Taking absolute values answers which features are repeatedly prominent, not whether they consistently raise the rain score. We used that prominence for pruning, while separate local plots and feature-bin patterns help recover some directional context. A feature can have a large absolute average even if its sign varies from one weather day to another.
ai_lime_samples: Five thousand was a fixed explanation setting, not a tested optimum. More synthetic samples might stabilize a surrogate but also increase computation, and the benefit depends on the underlying perturbation distribution. The ten-seed experiment tests one kind of randomness at that fixed sample count; it does not replace a sample-count sensitivity study.
ai_lime_seed: The stable top five and high rank agreement are reassuring for this particular configuration. But the borderline wind feature shows why a fixed cutoff and random variation should be reported together. I would distinguish stability of the broad ranking from stability of every individual inclusion decision or local weight magnitude.
ai_lime_vs_shap: A SHAP value and a LIME surrogate coefficient are not interchangeable units, even when both are displayed beside a weather feature. The two methods also depend on different background or perturbation assumptions. Our LIME paper mentions a separate SHAP companion study, so I would not infer a direct winner from comparing their reported numbers alone.
ai_precision_formula: For this hold-out, 73 days were called rainy by the baseline, and 59 of those calls were correct. The remaining 14 were false alarms. Precision therefore answers a concrete operational question: when this model issues a rain warning, how often was it right in this sample? It does not measure the rainy days the model missed.
ai_recall_formula: There were 72 actually rainy hold-out days. The baseline detected 59 and missed 13. Recall answers how much of the rain the system caught, which is different from whether every warning was trustworthy. A lower decision threshold might increase recall but could also produce more false alarms; that trade-off was not optimized for a user group here.
ai_f1_formula: The harmonic mean falls when either precision or recall is weak, so a model cannot get a high F1 by doing well on only one of them. The baseline calculation is tied to the chosen class cutoff and positive rain label. It does not summarize probability calibration or the cost of particular mistakes.
ai_aucpr_roc: AUC-PR is especially useful when the quality of positive rain warnings matters, whereas ROC AUC describes discrimination between the two classes more broadly. Both integrate across thresholds, unlike F1 at one cutoff. Because they answer different questions, a small improvement in one and decline in another is possible without contradiction.
ai_threshold_vs_auc: Moving only a few cases across the 0.5 boundary can improve the confusion matrix and its F1 while leaving the overall ordering of rain scores nearly unchanged or slightly worse. That is why we report both thresholded and ranking metrics. The observed differences are small and do not justify a claim that one path is generally superior.
ai_mcnemar_table: Only the disagreements contribute to McNemar's comparison. Days both models got right or both got wrong do not distinguish the two. The three-versus-one pattern favored Path A numerically, but with so few discordant cases it did not provide convincing statistical evidence of a performance difference.
ai_holm_steps: The practical reason is to avoid overclaiming after looking at several pairs. If we tested baseline versus A, baseline versus B, and A versus B independently at the same unadjusted threshold, the overall chance of a false finding would grow. In this paper the adjustment did not reveal any significant pairwise advantage.
ai_timeseries_split: Weather evolves through time, and later observations are the ones an operational forecast would encounter after training. Shuffling can let information from later conditions influence a model tested on earlier days. Our chronological split and expanding folds address that basic ordering issue, while the incomplete nesting of selection and tuning remains a separate concern.
ai_nested_cv: In a clean outer fold, no choice about features, hyperparameters, or a decision threshold should use that fold's test labels. Inner folds can make those choices using earlier training data. That separation is what would allow a less optimistic performance estimate. We did not complete that full nested design in this paper, so it is a concrete improvement for replication.
ai_cv_mean_vs_pooled: A small fold and a large fold receive equal weight in a simple mean of fold F1 values, while pooling predictions weights their actual case counts through the combined confusion matrix. The two summaries can therefore differ even with no calculation error. We should identify which definition is being quoted before comparing values across tables.
ai_bagging_boosting: For intuition, a random forest tries to stabilize predictions by averaging many partly independent trees, while boosting repeatedly improves an existing combined predictor. That distinction is algorithmic background. Our empirical comparison held XGBoost fixed and changed feature-refinement paths; it did not test whether bagging would outperform boosting on Bandung data.
ai_permutation_importance: Permutation importance asks how model performance changes when a feature's values are disrupted on a chosen evaluation set. That differs from tree-split gain and local LIME attribution, and correlated variables can complicate it too. It would be a useful additional comparator, but it was not in the reported experiment and should not be presented as an observed result.
ai_error_costs: For an outdoor event, missing rain may be worse than a false warning; for another operation, an unnecessary shutdown may cost more. The best cutoff depends on such consequences, not on F1 alone. Since our paper did not collect stakeholder cost estimates, we can report the confusion matrix but cannot claim one universally optimal operating point.
deep_xgb_regularization: The fair answer is to separate what XGBoost can do from what our experiment documented. Regularization exists in the algorithm, but we did not report an L1-versus-L2 study. The observed path differences therefore cannot be credited to a specific unreported penalty. We held the selected training setup common while changing the feature-refinement workflow.
deep_xgb_gamma: A stricter split rule could plausibly change both the fitted tree structures and gain importance values. That is why gamma would be a worthwhile sensitivity check if the study were extended. For this presentation, I would explain its general function and then state clearly that no gamma-specific finding appears in our reported results.
deep_xgb_minchild: This parameter is about the support required for a proposed child node, not a minimum number of weather variables. A higher setting can discourage fragile partitions, but the effect depends on the loss and data. Since we did not vary it experimentally, we should not assign any part of the reported F1 change to min_child_weight.
deep_xgb_leaf: The contribution from one leaf is only one term in a much larger ensemble score. It would be misleading to tell a listener that a single leaf is the whole forecast or a physical rule for rain. Our study summarizes performance and feature explanations at the model level, which is the level supported by the paper.
deep_xgb_margin: The distinction matters when discussing the 0.5 decision cutoff. A raw margin is not itself a 50% chance, and a transformed model output is not necessarily calibrated against real weather frequency. The paper gives predicted probabilities but does not document the exact internal link or a calibration test.
deep_xgb_gain_total: A feature used in one highly effective split can have impressive mean gain without dominating total gain across the ensemble. Conversely, frequent moderate splits can accumulate a large total. We chose a specific mean-gain summary for Path B, so any comparison with another importance definition must recompute the ranking rather than assume it is unchanged.
deep_xgb_gain_share: The denominator is the sum of mean-gain scores across included features. If the feature set or model fit changes, each share can change even when a variable still matters. That makes the 2% cutoff a reproducible rule within this setup, not a universal test of whether a weather variable is physically relevant.
deep_xgb_interactions: The engineered interaction could help a shallow tree access a useful pattern more easily, but that possibility is not the same as a measured improvement. To establish its individual contribution, we would retrain with and without that feature under the same split and settings. Our reported ablation does not isolate it on its own.
deep_xgb_correlation_gain: This is why I would avoid treating a difference between LIME and gain as evidence of a broken method. When predictors overlap, different importance definitions can assign credit to different members of a correlated group. The important empirical question is whether removing or changing the group affects out-of-time performance.
deep_xgb_seed: The distinction between explanation randomness and training randomness is easy to miss. Our ten runs held the underlying baseline model fixed and resampled the LIME process. They therefore support an explanation-rank stability statement, but not a claim that every independently retrained XGBoost model would yield the same ranking or score.
deep_xgb_monotonic: A positive relationship in a LIME display describes the fitted model locally; it does not mean we encoded a global monotonic law. Weather relationships can also interact with temperature and season. Before imposing a constraint, we would need to justify it physically and evaluate whether it helps or harms out-of-time predictions.
deep_xgb_train_eval: The key separation is that the final evaluation period should not steer the decisions being judged. We did use a later hold-out, but the hold-out feature vectors influenced the LIME aggregate ranking. That limits a strict prospective interpretation, even though the test labels were not used for that ranking.
deep_xgb_data_size: Three hundred trees do not mean three hundred independent observations per predictor, and there is no simple safe ratio that settles the question. What matters is how the fitted system behaves on later dates and across validation periods. Our checks are useful, but the limited station and selection design prevent a sweeping adequacy claim.
deep_xgb_class_weight: Because rain is not an extremely rare class in this cleaned sample, class weighting is not automatically necessary. It might trade fewer missed rainy days for more false alarms. That trade-off should be assessed with time-ordered validation and a stated user cost, rather than assuming a weighted model must be better.
deep_xgb_feature_order: For example, a column named RH_avg must have the same definition and units as it did during training, and rolling features must use only available history. This is an engineering requirement for any future deployment, not something validated by our paper's hold-out score. A schema check would catch many silent errors.
deep_lime_objective: The surrogate is optimized to mimic one model prediction's neighborhood, not to improve the underlying weather classifier. Its weights depend on the local samples, distance weighting, and simplicity constraint. That is why a high attribution should be interpreted as part of a local approximation, rather than as a direct objective improvement in XGBoost.
deep_lime_kernelwidth: A kernel-width sensitivity analysis would repeat explanations under several neighborhood sizes and compare rankings and local fit. We did not run that analysis, so I would avoid saying the selected neighborhood is uniquely correct. Seed stability under one width answers a narrower question than robustness to changing the width itself.
deep_lime_surrogate_type: The exact regressor matters because different simple models can approximate a nonlinear surface differently. We can explain the general local-surrogate idea confidently, but the paper's text does not justify naming a specific configured estimator. If asked for that implementation detail, checking the original code is the honest next step.
deep_lime_class: In a binary classifier, reversing the class being explained changes the interpretation of a positive or negative contribution. When presenting a plot, I would name the target class before reading any bar. Here the local-case discussion is about rain-class evidence, not a universal sign independent of output choice.
deep_lime_prediction: This distinction also explains the December case: its explanation changed after the feature set was revised, yet the classification did not. LIME can guide a later retraining decision, but running an explanation on an already fitted model is not itself an intervention that repairs a wrong forecast.
deep_lime_local_global: The aggregate is useful for a practical pruning rule, but it compresses many different weather days into one ordering. A feature can be important only in a particular season or can change sign across cases, and the absolute mean may hide that. It should be called an aggregate of local explanations.
deep_lime_rank_weight: A stable ordering means the same variables tend to appear near the top. It does not imply that every coefficient is numerically identical, nor that the explanation is faithful to XGBoost. Those are different quality criteria. We can report what our rank checks showed without stretching them into a stronger claim.
deep_lime_topk: This is a methodological ceiling of our aggregation procedure. A feature can receive zero in a particular case because it was outside the displayed top ten, not because XGBoost never used it. A full-feature explanation or alternative top-k setting would test how sensitive the pruning decision is to that display limit.
deep_lime_reference: The background distribution controls which synthetic cases the surrogate sees. If it includes information from later periods, or breaks relationships among correlated variables, the explanation can shift. Our reported paper does not provide enough constructor detail to make a stronger claim, so I would treat this as an open reproducibility question.
deep_lime_repeats: The repeated runs are useful because a ranking that changes drastically with one random draw would be a weak basis for feature removal. Here the major ranks were consistent, while one feature near the threshold varied. That nuance is more informative than saying simply that LIME was either perfectly stable or unstable.
deep_lime_local_case: This case is a clear reminder that explanation style and predictive correctness are separate outcomes. A more physically interpretable feature label can help a human understand a decision, but it does not guarantee a better decision. We use the example to illustrate representation, not to claim that the refinement fixed the false negative.
deep_lime_counterfactual: The weather variables also have dependencies: changing humidity alone while holding derived dew-point features fixed may create an impossible input. A causal or counterfactual claim would need a realistic intervention model and a different validation design. The safe LIME statement concerns the fitted classifier's local response to synthetic perturbations.
deep_lime_collinear: With correlation near minus one, the two signals almost mirror each other in this training set. A local linear surrogate can allocate apparent importance differently depending on sampling and representation. I would therefore discuss the humidity-related group, not insist that one coefficient measures a unique independent physical effect.
deep_lime_ood: This matters because the model may behave unpredictably on combinations never observed in training. LIME could then faithfully describe the model in an unrealistic region while still being a poor guide to actual weather. We did not quantify that in this study, so the explanation should not be used as causal proof.
deep_lime_fidelity_seed: A consistency check asks whether repeated explanations agree with one another. A fidelity check asks whether the surrogate actually reproduces the black-box model nearby. Both are important, but they are not interchangeable. We performed the former at the ranking level and should state plainly that the latter was not reported.
deep_lime_vs_gain_scope: The comparison becomes especially delicate when current humidity and its rolling average share information. One measure can emphasize local behavior on the chosen days, while another summarizes training-time splits. Rather than declaring one ranking true, we compared the resulting refinement paths and examined their out-of-time performance and limitations.
deep_lime_test_selection: Even unlabeled test inputs can reveal the distribution of the evaluation period. If they influence which features are kept, the resulting model has been adapted to that period in a way that would not be available for a truly unseen future period. A training-only LIME ranking inside each fold is the clean next test.
deep_lime_2percent: Sharing the number 2% keeps the procedure visually consistent, but it does not put the importance values on one scientific scale. This limitation compounds the unequal engineered feature pools. We can compare the practical paths under the stated rules, but should not claim a perfectly controlled causal contest between LIME and gain.
deep_eval_accuracy: I would show the confusion matrix rather than rely on one percentage. It tells the audience that the baseline missed 13 rainy days and issued 14 false rain alarms in the hold-out. Those errors matter differently to different users. An accuracy increase is only useful if we understand which mistakes changed.
deep_eval_pr_baseline: A no-skill PR reference follows the positive-class prevalence, so a PR area should not be interpreted without knowing how common rain was in the evaluation set. The prevalence differed between the cleaned dataset and the hold-out. For comparisons across cities or seasons, I would report that context rather than compare PR numbers in isolation.
deep_eval_roc_prevalence: This is especially relevant if rainy days become rare in a new application. A small false-positive rate can still create many false rain warnings when non-rain days dominate. ROC and PR curves should therefore be read together with class prevalence and the actual confusion matrix at the chosen threshold.
deep_eval_f1_limit: F1 can be useful for balancing missed rain against false alarms, but it treats their costs indirectly and ignores true negatives in its formula. A public warning system might prefer a different balance from a logistics planner. Our paper reports F1 as a research metric, not as proof that the operating threshold is optimal for any user.
deep_eval_threshold_tune: A clean procedure would tune the threshold inside a training-side time-series validation loop, lock it, and evaluate once on later untouched data. If we repeatedly adjust it after seeing the final hold-out results, the reported score becomes optimistic. We did not conduct that threshold-search experiment, so the 0.5 cutoff should be treated as a fixed choice.
deep_eval_auc_threshold: This distinction is why two models can have different F1 values at 0.5 yet nearly identical AUC values, or the reverse. An AUC does not tell us which cutoff a farmer should use. A deployment decision would still require calibration, costs, and a threshold chosen before the final evaluation.
deep_eval_confusion: Putting those counts into plain language helps: among the 72 rainy days, 13 rain events were missed; among the 57 dry days, 14 unnecessary rain alerts were made. That is more informative for discussion than saying only that 102 of 129 days were classified correctly. The counts also determine the reported precision, recall, and F1.
deep_eval_mcnemar_null: It does not compare two models trained on unrelated datasets, nor does it test every metric at once. The shared hold-out days make a paired comparison possible. In our baseline-versus-Path-A table, the discordant counts were three in one direction and one in the other, which was too small an imbalance to establish a difference.
deep_eval_mcnemar_f1: A change from a false positive to a correct dry prediction and a change from a false negative to a correct rain prediction can affect F1 differently. McNemar reduces both to correct versus incorrect. That is why its p-value should be presented as a paired error comparison, alongside the metric values rather than as a direct hypothesis test of F1.
deep_eval_pvalue: A p-value is calculated under a specified null model of the discordant outcomes. It is not the posterior probability that the null is true. With only four discordant days, the test has little information about a small effect. The conclusion is no detected difference, not proof that both paths are identically accurate.
deep_eval_power: This is a reason to avoid two opposite overclaims: saying the refined model definitely wins, or saying it definitely cannot help. The observed gain is small and uncertain. A longer untouched test period, more stations, or a preplanned confidence interval would help estimate how much improvement remains plausible.
deep_eval_type1: Holm adjustment addresses the fact that looking at several model pairs gives more opportunities for a chance finding. It is a safeguard against declaring victory from the smallest raw p-value alone. Since none of the adjusted comparisons was significant, the careful answer remains that no pair demonstrated a reliable predictive advantage.
deep_eval_wilcoxon_assumption: This check asks whether one path tends to have higher F1 across corresponding time periods, rather than pooling every daily prediction. It helps with one form of dependence, but expanding-window folds overlap in their training histories. I would treat its non-significant result as supporting caution, not as a perfect independent replication.
deep_eval_ttest_assumption: With only sixteen fold differences, the distributional assumptions deserve attention. The paired t-test and Wilcoxon pointing in the same non-significant direction is reassuring, but neither transforms overlapping folds into independent experiments. That is why I would report both as supplementary rather than use one p-value as a definitive answer.
deep_eval_serial: A rainy spell can create several related daily errors, so the number of independent pieces of information may be smaller than the count of days. This can affect uncertainty estimates. Fold-level comparisons were added as a second perspective, but a more rigorous design could use block-aware resampling or external periods.
deep_eval_fold_overlap: The folds are useful for seeing performance across several historical windows, but they share much of the same station series and increasingly large training sets. Their scores are therefore related. I would not call sixteen folds sixteen fully independent confirmations of the model's superiority or equivalence.
deep_eval_selection_bias: The risk is that settings look good partly because they were chosen with knowledge of periods later reported as validation. Nested time-series folds would repeat the choice inside each outer training window and evaluate on the untouched outer window. That would give a more defensible estimate of the entire modeling procedure.
deep_eval_feature_bias: The feature-selection step is itself a kind of learning. If it uses data from a future validation period, that fold is no longer a clean test of the selection pipeline. In a prospective evaluation, the ranking and pruning threshold would be applied using only data available before each fold's test period.
deep_eval_holdout_overlap: This overlap means the CV and hold-out results cannot be counted as two entirely independent pieces of evidence. The folds still cover more time than the final hold-out, so they have descriptive value. For a stronger claim, I would preserve a later period that neither tuning nor cross-validation ever touches.
deep_eval_missing_mechanism: If missing rainfall is related to station operation or particular weather conditions, simply deleting those days could change the class distribution and seasonal balance. We cannot infer that mechanism from the observed rows alone. The proper response is to audit the pattern and test sensitivity, not to claim the retained sample is automatically unbiased.
deep_eval_label_noise: This is especially relevant for very light rain near the boundary. A small measurement difference can flip the binary class even when the weather is nearly the same. We did not quantify how many days sit near 0.5 millimeters, so I would not invent a numerical impact; it is a limitation to test.
deep_eval_calibration_test: For example, if a group of days receives predictions around 70%, roughly seven in ten should actually be rainy for those probabilities to be well calibrated. That is a different claim from ranking rainy days above dry ones. Our paper does not test it, so I would avoid calling a single output a trustworthy real-world probability.
deep_eval_ci: A non-significant p-value alone leaves the size and direction of plausible effects unclear. An interval would make that uncertainty visible and help ask whether a practically meaningful gain is still compatible with the data. Since the paper did not report such an interval, I would not present a guessed range at the conference.
deep_eval_cost_curve: This makes the phrase best threshold incomplete unless we name a user and a cost model. We would collect or agree on the relative consequences, choose a cutoff on training-side validation data, and then test it on later days. The present study supplies confusion-matrix information, but not that operational decision analysis.
deep_eval_all_rain: This calculation gives a useful sanity reference because the hold-out had more rainy than dry days. An always-rain rule can obtain a nonzero F1 without learning useful weather patterns. The illustrative 0.716 is below the reported XGBoost baseline's 0.8138, but it was calculated from counts rather than run as a reported experiment.
deep_eval_threshold_curve: The exact precision-recall curve depends on the fitted model scores, so the direction of the trade-off is easier to state than a numerical result. Lower cutoffs generally catch more rain and warn more often. To choose a cutoff responsibly, we would need the complete curve, calibration checks, and user-specific error costs.
deep_eval_reproducibility: The key is to reproduce the whole sequence, not just the final XGBoost call. Row filtering, calendar alignment, imputation, feature engineering, explanation sampling, selection rules, and fold boundaries can all change the outcome. The paper gives substantial method detail, but an exact result would require the underlying code and data snapshot.
hypothesis: The practical test was not simply whether the final F1 number increased. We also asked whether the explanation-guided path could identify useful representations and remove less influential features without harming measured performance. The significance tests and ablation prevented us from claiming a LIME-caused accuracy advantage that the evidence did not support.
research_questions: Those questions lead to different forms of evidence: confusion matrices and validation scores for prediction, repeated LIME seeds for explanation stability, and ablation for attribution of the observed change. Keeping them separate helps avoid treating one attractive test score as proof that every part of the refinement workflow worked for the same reason.
not_accuracy_paper: A stronger forecasting paper would compare multiple model families and simple weather baselines on independent stations. Our design instead kept XGBoost common so we could study two feature-refinement paths. Forecast quality still matters, because a smaller model is not useful if it performs poorly, but state-of-the-art superiority was not the claim tested here.
falsification: A critical presentation should explain what the contrary result taught us. The ablation showed that cyclic encoding, rather than pruning alone, accounted for the hold-out F1 increase. We retained the more modest conclusion about explanation-driven diagnosis and parsimony instead of rewriting the hypothesis after seeing the results.
operational_scope: The output is a binary flag for the next observed day under the paper's data preparation. It does not give rainfall amount, hourly timing, or severe-weather probability. Before a user acts on it, we would also need to check when input measurements become available and how the user values false alarms versus missed rain.
data_provenance: The station identifier and the Kaggle route should both be stated, rather than saying we downloaded an official live BMKG feed. A direct official export would help verify records and timestamps. That matters especially because missing rainfall values and dropped days affect the forecasting horizon and the composition of the final sample.
missing_pattern: This is not a tiny random-looking gap. Two years had close to forty percent missing rainfall, so deleting missing-target rows can change which seasons and years dominate the training sample. The paper does not establish why those records are missing. We should treat representativeness as uncertain rather than assume the retained dates are unbiased.
row_counts: I would walk the audience through the sequence instead of quoting only the starting number. The classifier did not train on all 3,910 raw records. It used the processed sample after missing-target removal and feature construction. The paper does not provide a separate explanation for each of the final seven lost rows, so we should not invent one.
rain_prevalence: About three in five cleaned days were rainy, so a trivial tendency to predict rain often could achieve a superficially respectable accuracy. That is why we also examine precision, recall, F1, and AUC-PR. The hold-out class mix was slightly different, which should be remembered when comparing its metrics with the whole cleaned dataset.
seasonality: The annual pattern makes a calendar feature plausible, but it does not prove that the model learned a stable seasonal law. The cyclic transformation was tested because it better represents the calendar's wraparound. Its hold-out benefit still requires cautious interpretation because the paired differences were not statistically significant.
imputation_details: Using training-derived statistics avoids one direct leakage route from the final test period. It does not guarantee that simple averages or medians preserve all physical relationships, especially among derived humidity variables. We reported the rule used; a future sensitivity analysis could compare alternatives within time-ordered validation.
imputation_bias: The choice is a trade-off: a simple training-only fill is transparent and avoids using future values, but it can compress variation and create artificial combinations of weather features. We cannot quantify the resulting bias from this experiment. The honest next step is to compare several causal imputation strategies under the same chronological splits.
lag_construction: This distinction between row order and calendar time is essential. A lag of one observed row is not necessarily a lag of one day after missing rainfall rows are dropped. The features did not look into the future, yet some forecast horizons changed. A calendar-indexed preprocessing pipeline would address that issue more directly.
exact_day_subset: This subset check is reassuring in a limited sense: removing misaligned targets did not produce a significant pairwise winner. The F1 numbers changed because the evaluated days changed, so they are not directly interchangeable with the full 129-day hold-out scores. The models were not newly selected and tuned on only this subset.
previous_day_subset: The stricter rule removes still more observations, which reduces statistical power even as it improves temporal clarity. It is a sensitivity check, not a new deployment result. I would state the sample sizes and the unchanged non-significance conclusion rather than point to whichever model has the largest small-sample F1.
grid_search: The five-fold TimeSeriesSplit respected temporal ordering during parameter search, which is preferable to random folds for daily weather. The 54 combinations were evaluated with F1, then one configuration was used in all three feature paths. Because the entire later CV procedure was not fully nested around this search, its absolute scores still deserve caution.
fixed_hyperparams: This choice helps isolate the practical effect of changing features under one classifier setup. The cost is that each refined set may have a different best configuration that we did not search for. Retuning each path could improve its score, but would also require a nested design to keep the final comparison fair.
hyperparam_values: These are the values the audience can safely quote from the paper. We should separate them from XGBoost settings the paper did not specify, such as a particular gamma or L1 coefficient. The same reported configuration across paths makes the feature comparison easier to read, although it does not make the feature-engineering steps identical.
probability_cutoff: The two thresholds answer different questions and should not be confused. The 0.5-millimeter rule labels observed rain; the roughly 0.5 model-score cutoff turns a prediction into a class. Moving the second cutoff could trade recall against precision, but the paper does not report a tested alternative operating threshold.
calibration: A ranking metric can be strong even when the numerical probabilities are too high or too low. To use a 0.8 output as an 80% chance, we would need to compare predicted bins with observed frequencies on later data. The paper did not do that, so our confidence should be in the reported classification and ranking evaluation, not unverified probability calibration.
simple_baseline: Persistence and climatology are important checks before calling a model operationally superior. Their absence does not invalidate our within-XGBoost path comparison, but it narrows the claim. We can say how the three feature sets compared under the shared classifier; we cannot say this system beat every straightforward weather forecast.
class_weights: A roughly sixty-forty split is not extreme imbalance, but the costs of the two error types may still differ. Class weights could be tested in future work using only training-side validation. We should not imply that weighting or synthetic resampling was part of the reported pipeline when the paper does not say so.
feature_22: The baseline deliberately combines current-day measurements, recent history, and calendar information. Those groups serve different purposes: current conditions, short-term persistence, and seasonality. Listing them helps explain why later pruning and cyclic encoding are substantive changes rather than merely deleting arbitrary columns. It also reminds us that lag definitions depend on calendar alignment.
feature_path_a: The count of thirteen includes retained baseline measurements, two cyclic calendar coordinates, and three new weather-derived features. Those derived variables are functions of existing inputs, not independent new observations. We should therefore interpret their importance with attention to redundancy, especially the strong relationship between humidity and temperature–dew point spread.
feature_path_b: Path B is more than a list of variables discarded by gain. It also adds a humidity-trend feature derived from current and rolling humidity. Its fifteen predictors and Path A's thirteen are not identical candidate pools, so a score difference cannot be assigned solely to the choice of importance method.
rh_trend: A positive trend means current humidity sits above its recent mean, while a negative trend means it is below. That can give the classifier short-term context, but it is still derived from existing humidity measurements. The paper did not isolate the trend in a dedicated ablation, so its individual contribution to F1 remains uncertain.
sun_deficit: The plus-one in the denominator is an implementation safeguard, not a physical constant. The interaction was proposed as a potentially useful representation of humid, low-sunshine conditions. Because several features are correlated and the ablation did not isolate this one term, we cannot claim that the interaction alone caused the reported score change.
wind_encoding: I would avoid claiming the wind direction was perfectly represented. Wind angles are circular, while an arbitrary numeric category code may impose a false order. The study did not compare alternative wind encodings. A future test could use sine-cosine or one-hot representations under the same chronological evaluation.
lime_perturbations: Those settings define the explanation that was actually analyzed; changing any of them could change local weights. The 5,000 samples were not shown to be an optimum, and the top-ten display can omit a feature even if XGBoost uses it. The ten-seed stability study checks randomness within this fixed setup, not all possible explainer configurations.
lime_top_ten: This is why zero should be read as absent from the displayed local top ten, not as a proven zero effect. When averaged over 129 cases, repeated absence can reduce a feature's share below 2%. A sensitivity analysis with a different number of displayed features would test how robust that pruning rule is.
lime_weight_meaning: The denominator is the sum of absolute aggregate explanation weights for this model, data, and explainer setup. It is not a share of physical rainfall produced by humidity. The high percentage supports saying the classifier relied heavily on that signal, while correlated predictors and perturbation choices limit a stronger interpretation.
correlated_features: A local surrogate can allocate a shared signal among redundant columns in different ways. The almost perfect negative correlation between spread and RH_avg makes that issue concrete. I would discuss them as related representations of moisture rather than claim that each is an independent physical driver discovered by the model.
physics_check: A plausible story is a useful sanity check but not a fidelity score. A surrogate could produce a meteorologically sensible ranking while still approximating XGBoost poorly for a particular day. To establish that local quality, we would compare surrogate and classifier outputs around the explained instances; that analysis was not reported.
quartile_thresholds: If the reference data changed, the quartile boundaries could move. The labels are useful for explaining which region of humidity the model saw, but they are not a law that rain begins above exactly one number. We should describe them as LIME bins tied to this dataset.
gain_definition: Mean gain is a training-time summary over tree splits, while LIME asks about prediction behavior near selected inputs. Normalizing each into shares makes a 2% pruning rule possible within each path, but does not turn the two methods into identical scales. Correlation and feature engineering can make their rankings differ legitimately.
gain_ranking: Both methods point toward humidity-related information, which is a useful consistency check. Their top individual variable differs partly because current and rolling humidity overlap. I would not infer that the 21.6% versus 21.3% gain shares are causal fractions, nor that the small ranking difference proves one method wrong.
path_a_compactness: The practical gain is a simpler input set under this specific evaluation, not a proven increase in forecast skill. Nine fewer predictors may help interpretation and data collection, but the paper did not benchmark deployment cost or prove strict equivalence. I would present the smaller model and the uncertainty in predictive difference together.
ten_feature_variant: This sensitivity check suggests that several raw measurements are redundant with derived representations in the fitted setup. It does not mean the original sensors are unnecessary: the derived features still depend on those measurements. The result is limited to this station, split, and configuration, and the reported statistical comparison did not establish a reliable performance difference.
pruning_nine: The important nuance is that pruning alone preserved the baseline hold-out F1; it did not create the full Path A numerical lift. The nine-feature result supports model simplification, while cyclic encoding explains the hold-out gain seen in the ablation. Those are two different contributions that should not be merged into one exaggerated LIME accuracy claim.
auc_metrics: AUC metrics summarize the ordering of scores across thresholds, while F1 uses one operating cutoff. Therefore Path B can lead the AUC values and Path A can lead F1 without contradiction. The numerical gaps are small, and no paired test in the study established that one refinement path is predictively superior overall.
precision_recall_tradeoff: The changes are more informative when tied to the actual hold-out days than when presented as a dramatic percentage gain. A few corrected or newly wrong days can move both fractions. We did not optimize a stakeholder-specific error cost, so we should report the observed precision and recall rather than claim the new balance is universally preferable.
pooled_vs_mean: This is a mathematical difference, not evidence that one table is wrong. A mean gives each fold score a place in an average; a pooled calculation combines all prediction counts before computing the nonlinear ratio. When presenting, I would say which F1 definition I am quoting and avoid mixing the 0.828 mean with the roughly 0.84 pooled values.
holm: With three comparisons, correcting for multiplicity prevents us from cherry-picking whichever raw test looked most favorable. Adjusted values of 1.000 do not prove identical models; they mean the observed paired differences did not pass this family-wise significance test. That is consistent with the cautious conclusion drawn from fold-level comparisons.
wilcoxon: A fold-level test asks whether one path tends to outperform another over corresponding historical windows. It is a useful second perspective because pooled days may be serially related. However, the expanding folds share training history, so the sixteen differences are not perfect independent replications. The result adds caution, not proof of equality.
equivalence: This statistical distinction is worth saying plainly to an audience: failing to reject a difference is not the same as demonstrating equivalence. To claim equivalence, we would first state how large a difference is acceptable in practice and then test whether the data rule out larger differences. We did not do that analysis.
effect_size: The net improvement of two correctly classified days is understandable, but it is small relative to the 129-day sample. That makes uncertainty and error type important. We can report the observed F1 increase and the three-corrected, one-new-error pattern, while avoiding a claim that such a gain will persist in future years or stations.
confidence_interval: An interval would help distinguish a result that is merely inconclusive from one that already rules out a practically useful gain. Because we did not report one, I would not invent bounds during Q&A. The honest answer is that the point estimate is small and the paired tests were non-significant, while its precise uncertainty range remains unreported.
official_forecast: Official weather services combine broader observations, expert procedures, and responsibilities that this single-station research model was not designed to replace. Our output can be studied as a decision-support signal under the stated daily target. External validation, calibration, input-timing checks, and operational review would be needed before any real-world substitution claim.
out_of_scope_hourly: An hourly storm-warning system would need observations and targets at an hourly or finer scale, likely including information unavailable in this daily station table. A model evaluated on next-day binary rain cannot be assumed to resolve timing within the day. We list nowcasting as a future direction, not a capability demonstrated here.
heavy_rain: The binary label puts a 0.5-millimeter day and a much wetter day in the same positive class. A good F1 for that label therefore says nothing direct about detecting extremes. A heavy-rain study would define a separate threshold or amount target and evaluate errors specifically for severe events.
literature_gap: The distinctive part is the feedback loop: use explanation results to reconsider representation and pruning, then compare that path with the model's own importance measure under paired evaluation. The ablation and non-significant tests make the conclusion more restrained than a simple claim that XAI raises accuracy. We should present the actual tested gap, not a sweeping novelty claim.
companion_status: The safest presentation practice is to label slide figures from the SHAP work as separate context. They can motivate discussion about explanation methods, but the LIME paper's conclusions rest on its own baseline, Path A, Path B, ablation, and significance results. We should not merge unpublished companion results into the primary evidence without saying so.
no_pressure: A feature absent from the dataset cannot be ranked by LIME or gain within the fitted model. It might add useful information, but it might not; the paper contains no experiment answering that. The right next step would be to obtain those measurements with appropriate timing and test them under the same chronological evaluation.
input_timing: A forecast called next-day is only operational if all current-day inputs are already available at the moment the prediction is issued. Some daily summaries may be finalized later. The paper does not map that release schedule, so it reports a retrospective classification experiment rather than a verified real-time forecast service.
test_imputation: This is an example where we can state a concrete safeguard: test values did not determine the fill statistics. It does not settle every leakage concern. Feature selection, the use of unlabeled hold-out inputs for LIME ranking, and incomplete nesting of cross-validation still limit how independent the reported evaluations are.
local_explanation: The strongest negative contribution in the plot says the fitted classifier associated that humidity bin with a lower rain score around this case. It does not tell us the full physical cause of the next day's rain. The example also remained wrong after Path A, so it illustrates explanation behavior rather than a corrected forecast.
rh_monotonic: The aggregate quartile pattern is not a guarantee that the full XGBoost prediction is globally monotonic in humidity for every combination of other conditions. We did not impose a monotonic constraint or test every possible weather state. I would describe the observed explanation trend, with the bins tied to this data.
point_biserial: A marginal correlation is a useful plausibility check: it asks whether each feature alone moves with the binary target in the observed sample. It does not account for all other correlated features or prove a causal effect. Agreement with LIME can support a coherent story, but it cannot replace a local-fidelity test.
wind_borderline: The 1.89% value used in one run sat only slightly below the 2% rule, and most seed runs actually placed the feature above the boundary. That is why we call this particular exclusion fragile. A different seed or cutoff might retain it, even though the broader top-feature ranking was stable.
topfive_jaccard: Jaccard one compares sets: it tells us the same five feature identities appeared at the top, regardless of their internal order or exact weights. It is strong evidence of set stability under the ten tested seeds. It is not evidence that every local explanation is faithful or that those features cause rainfall.
kendall_spearman: The two measures provide related but distinct checks of ordering agreement. A high value for both means the seed runs gave similar rank patterns under the fixed setup. Neither assesses whether synthetic perturbations are physically realistic, whether the surrogate fits XGBoost locally, or whether the result transfers to another station.
exact_mcnemar: When discordant cases are scarce, a large-sample approximation can be unreliable. The exact binomial calculation is then the more appropriate way to assess the paired imbalance. Our hold-out comparisons had only a few changed outcomes, so it is especially important not to overread a small numerical score difference.
paired_t: The agreement of several non-significant tests is useful as a consistency check, but these fold scores came from one station time series with overlapping expanding training windows. The paired t-test also assumes an appropriate distribution of fold differences. I would not present its p-values as sixteen independent replications proving equivalence.
cv_overlap: The overlap does not make the folds useless; they still show performance across a broader sequence of periods. It does mean we cannot add the hold-out and CV results together as though they were fully independent confirmations. A later untouched period would be a clearer final test after model choices are fixed.
nested_selection: The key idea is to evaluate the full procedure a future user would actually run, not just a model after it has benefited from later data. Every outer fold must hide its test period from tuning and feature choice. Our current folds do not meet that ideal completely, so a nested rerun could change the absolute scores.
holdout_features: The issue is subtle because no hold-out labels were used for that ranking. However, the input distribution of the test period still guided which features Path A kept. That makes the feature set partly adapted to the period being judged. The proposed repair is to compute explanations and select features from training data only.
runtime_cost: Thousands of perturbation predictions per explained day can add substantial work, but the paper gives no timing or resource benchmark. We should therefore describe LIME as an offline diagnosis and model-refinement tool in this study, not claim that its explanation step is fast enough for real-time deployment without measurement.
lime_fidelity: Stability and fidelity answer different questions. Ten seeds can yield similar rankings even if a local surrogate poorly matches XGBoost near some days. A future study should report local fit quality and flag weak approximations before using their weights for interpretation or pruning. We did not calculate those scores here.
outside_scope: This is a good place to be direct in Q&A. I would name the missing experiment, say what this paper actually measured, and describe the design needed to answer the new question. I would not invent an accuracy, runtime, or causal effect simply because an audience member asks for one.
honest_takeaway: The most defensible answer separates three observations: the explanation ranking was stable under tested seeds, the model could be made smaller, and the observed hold-out F1 lift was driven by cyclic encoding without a significant overall advantage. That gives a useful research conclusion without claiming operational superiority or universal transfer.
